strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful auditing problem: quantifying deviation from multiclass equalized odds, including when only aggregate statistics are available. Extending the population-weighted contamination interpretation of Sabato and Yom-Tov (2020) is a useful contribution.

Theorem 4.1 provides a sound multiclass characterization, and Equation (7) yields an efficiently computable lower bound. The label-merging argument gives a principled basis for greedy initialization, while feasible baseline assignments provide upper bounds without requiring global optimization.

The known-confusion-matrix experiments demonstrate practical value across two datasets and three classifier families. Greedy initialization plus local optimization generally improves the upper bounds, with particularly tight intervals on several Natality experiments. The detailed formulations, appendices, and linked code support understanding and reproduction.
weaknesses: The central aggregate-only accuracy claim is not adequately validated. Although Section 7 promises tight upper/lower bounds in both regimes, Tables 2 and 7–10 report local-optimization upper bounds on minDCP without corresponding minDCP lower bounds. Comparing these values with the actual classifier's DCP interval does not establish proximity to the minimum over compatible classifiers. A large upper bound on minDCP cannot certify substantial unfairness. Consequently, the election and education interpretations are not supported by demonstrated optimization accuracy.

The statistical robustness assertion in Sections 4 and 7.1 requires a specified error metric and proof; interpreting DCP as a population fraction does not establish it. Under total variation, the assertion is false even in the binary special case: with equally weighted groups and prediction rates independent of the true label, changing one group's rate from 0.50 to 0.51 changes the joint distribution by 0.005 but increases DCP from zero to approximately 0.0098. Sampling uncertainty is not quantified, and clipping confusion probabilities or modifying marginals changes the optimization problem without an accompanying bound on the resulting error.

Appendix D contains a concrete error in its convergence discussion. Equation (18) is not jointly convex in its two optimized arguments: on b < a, the function a² − ab has an indefinite Hessian. Thus Figure 4 does not validate convergence on the claimed convex problem. The applicability of the cited convergence guarantees to the implemented constraint-dropping and step-size rules also needs justification. This does not invalidate feasible upper bounds, but it weakens the optimization guarantees.

The numerical evaluation compares primarily internal initialization variants, without runtime/scaling results or comparisons against standard constrained optimizers. Some certified intervals remain substantially wide—for example, 8.29%–23.61% in Table 1. Small instances with independently established optima would help distinguish loose analytical bounds from poor local optimization and clarify when the proposed method is reliable.

Smaller presentation and reproducibility gaps include unnamed Census prediction targets in rows identified only by their number of labels, missing train/test partition details and subgroup sample counts, and insufficiently explicit implementation details for the aggregate-only lower bound. These are correctable, but the aggregate-only validation and robustness issues above affect the principal research conclusions and motivate weak rejection.
